rationale: Dropping unsolicited packets to stop port scans and flooding is resistance to network attacks.
Lockout after consecutive failed sign-ins contains brute-force attacks (rule 1) and no credential verification is mentioned.
Pages are prevented from reading or altering stored credentials and profiles, covering both disclosure and modification.
A check detects whether stored records were altered since an authorised write, which is integrity.
Only controllers with write privilege may create amendments, restricting who can modify data (rule 3).
Changes to templates are restricted to the chief physician, a restriction on who can modify.
Inactivity timeout to prevent misuse of an abandoned browser limits abuse exposure (rule 7).
Validating the certificate chain and host name verifies the website is who it claims to be.
Detecting tampering with model files or hostile-input halts and returning to a clean configuration is a safe state under attack, and covers manipulated files.
Admitting a clinician only with a registered secret is credential-based authentication.
Users without admin rights are barred from creating, editing or deleting records; viewing is permitted so no read restriction is expressed.
Rejecting invalid values and leaving the dataset unchanged validates data correctness and protects the dataset.
A passphrase must be supplied before the profile email can be modified, guarding modification and verifying the customer.
Schema and checksum validation protect data, and blocking and flagging writes showing deliberate tampering resists attack.
Encryption prevents eavesdroppers from interpreting flight-plan updates (rule 5).
Users must prove identity with valid credentials before recording, which is authentication.
Payee list changes only occur after explicit holder approval, preventing unauthorised modification.
Only editors may trim, annotate or delete recordings, restricting who can modify.
Third parties must not be able to evade or disable fraud-detection and brute-force protections, preserving attack defences.
User scripts must not deactivate attack-detection and lockdown mechanisms, keeping the system defended under attack.
Terminals must prove identity with a valid certificate, which is device authentication.
Credentials are verified against the stored account before granting access, which is authentication.
Operator identity is verified against the directory before launching a run.
Public-key encryption so only the operator's private key can decrypt travel documents protects confidentiality.
Each user must sign in with a unique individual account identifier before uploading, which is identification and authentication.
The claimed origin of each feed is verified with the source's registered certificate.
Confirming the login secret matches the registered one is credential verification.
Checksum verification rejects object files that differ from what was produced, detecting alteration.
Detecting anomalous scanning traffic and blocking its source is attack detection and blocking.
Sign-in relies on an identity assertion from a third-party identity provider, which is authentication.
Only the entering user may change parameters and only after identity verification, restricting modification and requiring identity checks.
Preventing pages from enumerating internal hosts withholds network information from untrusted content and blocks reconnaissance.
Blocking unsolicited inbound internet traffic is stateful perimeter defence against attacks.
Balance consistency under concurrency and restricting changes to authorised terminals protects data from corruption and unauthorised modification.
Pages and unapproved extensions are prevented from altering bookmarks and settings, protecting data from modification.
A keyed HMAC tag with reporting of mismatches detects alteration of job record files.
Re-confirming identity through challenge questions is authentication; protection of card data is only implied.
Only data stewards may roll back a committed load to a consistent state, restricting who can modify data.
Access is granted only when the supplied identity matches a registered customer, which is authentication.
